reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Presents in early infancy with hypotonia, developmental delay, movement disorder and characteristic oculogyric crises
Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in DDC, encoding aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that makes dopamine and serotonin
Autonomic features are prominent: ptosis, nasal congestion, excessive sweating, temperature instability and feeding difficulties
Symptoms often show a diurnal pattern, being worse towards the end of the day
The diagnostic CSF neurotransmitter profile shows low homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid with a raised 3-O-methyldopa, alongside reduced plasma AADC enzyme activity and elevated L-dopa
Diagnosis rests on CSF neurotransmitter metabolites, reduced plasma AADC enzyme activity and DDC genetic testing
Treatment is challenging and may combine dopamine agonists, monoamine oxidase inhibitors and pyridoxal phosphate, with gene therapy now an important disease-modifying option
Because AADC acts downstream of L-dopa, levodopa alone is generally ineffective, unlike in dopa-responsive dystonia
reference.pathophysiology: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) catalyses the final step in the synthesis of the monoamine neurotransmitters, converting L-dopa to dopamine and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin. Biallelic DDC variants reduce enzyme activity, so dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline and serotonin are all deficient. The resulting monoamine deficiency produces a movement disorder with oculogyric crises, hypotonia, developmental delay and autonomic dysfunction. Because the block is at the decarboxylation step, upstream substrates such as L-dopa and its methylated derivative 3-O-methyldopa accumulate while the downstream metabolites homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid fall, giving the diagnostic CSF pattern. Management aims to boost residual monoamine signalling and, increasingly, to restore enzyme activity through gene therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Dopa-responsive dystonia and tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency
Cerebral palsy and other static encephalopathies
Epileptic encephalopathies (oculogyric crises can mimic seizures)
additionalInvestigations: CSF neurotransmitter metabolites (low HVA and 5-HIAA, raised 3-O-methyldopa)
Plasma and CSF amino acids including L-dopa
EEG to distinguish oculogyric crises from seizures
redFlags: Prolonged or distressing oculogyric crises with autonomic storm
reference.prognosis: Untreated severe disease causes marked disability, but multi-agent pharmacotherapy and, in particular, gene therapy can produce meaningful gains in motor function and quality of life, so outcome depends on phenotype severity and access to treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking oculogyric crises for epileptic seizures and escalating antiepileptics
Expecting levodopa alone to work as it does in dopa-responsive dystonia
Missing the diagnosis without CSF neurotransmitter studies
Under-recognising the autonomic features and their acute risks
references: GeneReviews / OMIM entry for AADC Deficiency (DDC)
management: Putaminal gene therapy replacing DDC is the emerging disease-specific treatment, offering meaningful improvement in motor function
Multi-agent pharmacotherapy to boost residual monoamine signalling, combining dopamine agonists, monoamine oxidase inhibitors and pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)
Anticholinergic drugs to ease dystonia and oculogyric crises
Supportive treatment of autonomic dysfunction, including ptosis, temperature instability, sweating and feeding difficulty
Nutritional support and management of gastrointestinal dysmotility, with gastrostomy where oral intake is unsafe
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive DDC disorder, with confirmatory molecular testing and cascade family screening
Coordinate multidisciplinary care with metabolic medicine, neurology, physiotherapy and dietetics
